stories.topicLabel: Abdul El-Sayed Michigan Senate race and Democrats
stories.analysis: Coverage of Abdul El-Sayed's Michigan Senate race was largely uniform across outlets, with a bias spread of just one point separating the most-left and most-right framing. Both headlines center on Democratic Party unity as the core political stakes. NPR's framing was the more neutral of the two, using straightforward descriptive language — "split" and "unify" — to characterize intraparty tension without assigning sympathy or blame to any faction. Vox moved slightly left not by distorting facts but by narrowing its lens to a specific subgroup, "Jewish Democrats," and employing the phrase "trying to get to 'yes,'" which carries an implicit sympathetic framing toward El-Sayed's candidacy by portraying hesitant supporters as working toward acceptance rather than expressing principled opposition. That tonal difference is modest, and both outlets share the same fundamental neutral premise: Democratic cohesion around El-Sayed will shape Senate control.
